Every Saturday morning, Mei Ling goes to the hawker centre with her grandfather. They always arrive at seven o'clock, before the crowd comes. Grandfather likes to sit at the same table near the fan, beside the stall that sells soya bean milk.
Today, Mei Ling queued at the porridge stall while Grandfather saved the seats. The queue was short, but the auntie behind the counter was slow because she was stirring a huge pot. Mei Ling waited patiently and counted the ceiling fans to pass the time. When it was her turn, she ordered two bowls of fish porridge and one extra egg.
On the way back to the table, she carried the tray with both hands. A boy ran past and nearly knocked into her. Mei Ling's heart thumped, but she held on tightly and not a drop was spilled. Grandfather clapped softly when she put the tray down. "Steady hands," he said, smiling. "You will make a fine waitress one day." Mei Ling laughed and said she would rather be a doctor. They ate slowly, and Grandfather told her about the kampong where he first ate porridge as a boy. By eight o'clock, the tables were full, and it was time to go home.

Where does Grandfather like to sit?
options: Beside the porridge stall where Mei Ling queues
At the table closest to the hawker centre entrance
Outside the hawker centre, under a shady tree
Near the fan, beside the soya bean milk stall

explain.why: Mei Ling queued at the porridge stall, but Grandfather's table is near the fan, beside the soya bean milk stall.
The passage never mentions the entrance. It says his usual table is near the fan.
Grandfather sits inside, at 'the same table near the fan'. No tree is mentioned.

solution: Grandfather likes to sit at the same table near the fan, beside the stall that sells soya bean milk.
This sentence gives his usual seat.

At recess on Monday, Ryan could not find his new water bottle. It was blue with a picture of a shark, and his father had given it to him on his birthday only last week. Ryan was sure he had left it on the bench in the canteen, but the bench was empty.
He searched under the tables and behind the rubbish bins. He even asked the drink stall uncle, but the uncle shook his head. Ryan's stomach felt heavy. He was afraid his father would be disappointed in him.
After school, Ryan walked slowly along the corridor towards the school gate. Mr Salim, the school cleaner, was pushing his cart. "Looking for something, young man?" he asked. Ryan told him about the bottle. Mr Salim smiled and lifted a cloth on his cart. There, between the brooms, was the blue shark bottle. "I found it on the bench after recess," he said. "I kept it safe because I knew someone would come back for it."
Ryan could hardly speak. He said thank you three times. The next morning, he gave Mr Salim a packet of biscuits from his mother. This time, Ryan wrote his name in big black letters on the bottle.

What did Ryan's water bottle look like?
options: Silver, with a blue lid
Blue, with a picture of a whale
Red, with his name on it
Blue, with a picture of a shark

explain.why: The passage says the bottle is blue with a shark picture. It does not mention silver or a lid.
The picture is of a shark, not a whale.
The bottle is blue. Ryan wrote his name on it only after it was found.

solution: It was blue with a picture of a shark, and his father had given it to him on his birthday only last week.
This sentence describes the bottle.

Mangroves are trees that grow in muddy places where the sea meets the land. In Singapore, you can find them at Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve and on Pulau Ubin. Most trees would die in salty water, but mangrove trees have special roots that help them survive. Some roots grow up out of the mud like pencils so that the tree can breathe when the tide is high. Other roots spread out wide and hold the tree firmly in the soft ground.
Mangroves are home to many animals. Mudskippers, small fish that can climb onto the mud, hop about at low tide. Crabs hide in holes between the roots, and birds such as herons stand quietly in the shallows, waiting for a meal. Young fish also shelter among the roots, where bigger fish cannot reach them easily.
Mangroves are also useful to people. Their thick roots slow down the waves, so the shore is not washed away so quickly. Because of this, many countries are now planting mangroves again.
Visitors to the reserve walk along a wooden boardwalk. Rangers ask them to speak softly and not to feed the animals, so that the creatures can live as they would in the wild.

How do the roots that grow up like pencils help a mangrove tree?
options: They hold the tree firmly in the soft ground
They catch small fish for the tree to eat
They store fresh water for the dry season
They let the tree breathe at high tide

explain.why: That is the job of the roots that spread out wide, not the pencil-like ones.
Trees do not eat fish, and the passage does not say this.
The passage says nothing about storing water.

solution: Some roots grow up out of the mud like pencils so that the tree can breathe when the tide is high.
The sentence names the purpose of the pencil-like roots.

Mum's birthday was on Sunday, and Daniel and his younger sister Kai Xin wanted to surprise her with a cake. While Mum was at work on Saturday, they took out the flour, eggs and butter. Dad promised to help, but he stayed in the living room reading the newspaper, because he wanted the children to do most of it themselves.
Daniel measured the flour carefully. Kai Xin cracked the eggs, and some shell fell into the bowl, so they picked it out with a spoon. They poured the mixture into a tin and put it in the oven. Forty minutes later, a sweet smell filled the flat. "It's ready!" Kai Xin shouted. But when Daniel opened the oven, the middle of the cake had sunk into a deep dip.
Kai Xin's lip trembled. "We ruined it." Daniel stared at the cake. Then he had an idea. He filled the dip with whipped cream and covered it with sliced strawberries until it looked like a little garden.
On Sunday evening, Mum blew out the candles. "The dip is the best part," she laughed, taking a big spoonful of cream and strawberries. "It's like a secret surprise inside." Kai Xin grinned and whispered to Daniel, "Next year, let's make the dip on purpose."

What went wrong with the cake?
options: Eggshell was left in the mixture
The middle sank into a deep dip
It did not rise because the eggs were forgotten
The outside was burnt black

explain.why: Some shell fell in, but they picked it out with a spoon before baking.
Kai Xin cracked the eggs and they were added to the mixture.
A sweet smell filled the flat, and the problem was a dip in the middle, not burning.

solution: But when Daniel opened the oven, the middle of the cake had sunk into a deep dip.
This sentence names the problem.

Daniel measured the flour carefully. Kai Xin cracked the eggs, and some shell fell into the bowl, so they picked it out with a spoon. They poured the mixture into a tin and put it in the oven. Forty minutes later, a sweet smell filled the flat. "It's ready!" Kai Xin shouted. But when Daniel opened the oven, the middle of the cake had sunk into a deep dip.
Kai Xin's lip trembled. "We ruined it." Daniel stared at the cake. Then he had an idea. He filled the dip with whipped cream and covered it with sliced strawberries until it looked like a little garden.
On Sunday evening, Mum blew out the candles. "The dip is the best part," she laughed, taking a big spoonful of cream and strawberries. "It's like a secret surprise inside." Kai Xin grinned and whispered to Daniel, "Next year, let's make the dip on purpose."

Why does the writer include Mum's words, "It's like a secret surprise inside"?
options: To show that Mum was hiding her anger
To show that Mum did not notice the cake had gone wrong
To show that Mum liked cream more than cake
To show Mum saw the mistake cheerfully

explain.why: She laughed and took a big spoonful. Nothing suggests she was angry.
Mum saw the dip, because she said 'The dip is the best part'.
Her words are about the dip being a happy surprise, not about preferring cream.

solution: "The dip is the best part," she laughed, taking a big spoonful of cream and strawberries.
Mum turns the mistake into something nice, which shows a kind and cheerful attitude.

On Wednesday afternoon, forty Primary 4 pupils crowded into the school hall for the badminton try-outs. Jia Hui stood at the back with her racket. Her hands were cold and her mouth was dry. Only twelve pupils would be chosen for the team.
Coach Ong divided the pupils into groups. In Jia Hui's first rally, she missed the shuttlecock twice. Her cheeks burned as a girl on the next court giggled. Jia Hui wanted to put down her racket and walk out.
"Everyone, watch your feet," called Coach Ong. "Good players are always moving, even when they are waiting." Jia Hui remembered that her older brother had told her the same thing. She bent her knees, rocked on her toes and watched the shuttlecock closely. This time she swung early and sent it back over the net. Her partner whooped. They kept the rally going for eleven hits before it fell.
At the end of the session, Coach Ong pinned a list on the board. Jia Hui's name was ninth. She did not shout. She only pressed her lips together and smiled so widely that her cheeks hurt. "Thank you, Coach," she said. "Come on time on Friday," he replied, "and bring water."

How many pupils would be chosen for the team?
options: Eleven
Twelve
Forty
Nine

explain.why: Eleven is the number of hits in the rally.
Forty is the number of pupils who came to the try-outs, not the number to be chosen.
Jia Hui's name was ninth on the list. That is her place, not the number chosen.

solution: Only twelve pupils would be chosen for the team.
The sentence gives the number.

Many HDB blocks in Singapore have blue recycling bins on the ground floor. Families put their old paper, plastic bottles, cans and glass in them, so that these things can be made into new products instead of being thrown away.
Before you recycle, there are three simple steps. First, empty the container. Second, rinse it with a little water, because food left inside can make other items dirty. Third, dry it and drop it into the bin. Do not put the items into a plastic bag, because the workers at the sorting centre may not open the bag and the contents may be thrown away.
Some things cannot be recycled in the blue bin. Used tissues, oily pizza boxes and broken mirrors should go into the normal rubbish chute. Oil and food soak into paper, which makes it hard to turn it into clean new paper.
Last year, Class 5C tried a challenge. Each pupil brought clean recyclables from home for one month. At the end, the class had filled twelve large boxes with bottles and old newspapers. "We never knew our rubbish could be useful," said Ahmad, the class monitor. The class has decided to continue the habit every term.

Which of these should go into the normal rubbish chute?
options: An empty glass jar
A drink can that has been rinsed
A pizza box soaked in oil
An old newspaper

explain.why: Glass is listed as something to recycle.
Cans are listed as things that go into the blue bin.
Old paper belongs in the blue bin.

solution: Used tissues, oily pizza boxes and broken mirrors should go into the normal rubbish chute.
The sentence lists oily pizza boxes among the things that cannot be recycled.

Everyone in Block 214 knew that the old man in the corner flat was grumpy. Mr Rahman never smiled at the lift lobby, and when the children played football downstairs, he would frown from his window and shut it with a bang. Haikal and his friends called him "the Wall".
One evening, Haikal's mother was stuck at work, and he came home to find he had forgotten his key. The corridor was dark and he did not want to wait alone on the cold floor. Just then, Mr Rahman's door opened. "Why are you sitting there?" the old man asked gruffly. Haikal explained. Mr Rahman said nothing, but he pointed to a stool beside his door and went back inside.
A few minutes later, he returned with a glass of warm Milo and two biscuits. "You'll catch a cold," he muttered. Haikal noticed photographs on the wall behind him: a young man holding a football trophy, then a boy about Haikal's age kicking a ball on a field. "My son," said Mr Rahman, following his gaze. "He played every evening until he moved overseas." His voice softened. "The noise downstairs... I used to love it. Now it only makes the flat feel quiet."
When Haikal's mother arrived, she thanked Mr Rahman warmly. The next week, Haikal knocked on the old man's door with his football under his arm. "Uncle, would you like to watch us play? We'll keep the noise down." Mr Rahman looked at the ball and almost smiled. "You needn't," he said. "Make all the noise you like."

Why was Haikal sitting in the corridor?
options: He was waiting for Mr Rahman to come home
He had forgotten his key
His mother had locked him out as a punishment
He was hiding from his friends

explain.why: Mr Rahman was already at home and opened his door after seeing Haikal.
His mother was stuck at work. He was locked out because of his own forgotten key.
The passage never says he was hiding. He did not want to wait alone.

solution: One evening, Haikal's mother was stuck at work, and he came home to find he had forgotten his key.
This sentence explains why he could not enter the flat.

At many hawker centres, a familiar sight greets diners after the lunch rush: tables piled with empty bowls, chopsticks and half-finished drinks. Cleaners hurry from table to table, but they cannot keep up. Since June, the town council has placed bright yellow signs at every table asking customers to return their trays, and the results have been mixed.
Supporters say the idea is simple. When diners return trays, cleaners can spend their time wiping tables and mopping floors instead of carrying dishes. The next customer also finds a clean table sooner. In the first month, a pilot study at the Block 85 hawker centre found that tables were ready for new diners almost twice as quickly.
Not everyone is happy, however. Some elderly diners find it hard to carry a heavy tray across a crowded floor. A few stallholders worry that customers who have to walk to the return point will choose to eat elsewhere. A cleaner, Madam Tan, says that she is glad for the help. "Some people leave the tray right beside the return rack, just one step away," she says. "It takes the same effort to put it back properly."
Perhaps the answer is to keep the habit but make it easier. The council is now adding return points near the entrance and has promised that staff will carry trays for elderly diners who ask.

What did the pilot study at Block 85 find?
options: Fewer diners came to the hawker centre
Stallholders sold twice as much food that day
Cleaners worked fewer hours each week
Tables were ready almost twice as quickly

explain.why: This is a worry raised by some stallholders. The study did not find it.
Sales are not mentioned in the study.
The study measured how quickly tables became ready, not the cleaners' hours.

solution: In the first month, a pilot study at the Block 85 hawker centre found that tables were ready for new diners almost twice as quickly.
This sentence states the result of the pilot study.

options: He walked to the front and read her notes aloud
He told the boy in the back row to stop laughing
He mouthed a hint to start with the fish
He asked Ms Chen to give her more time

explain.why: He stayed in his seat and only mouthed a few words.
Wei Jie 'did not laugh', but he did not scold anyone.
Wei Jie never spoke to Ms Chen.

solution: He caught her eye and mouthed, "Start with the fish."
This sentence shows exactly how he helped.

The Robotics Club had spent three months building a robot that could pick up plastic cups and stack them into a tower. On the morning of the inter-school competition, the team stood nervously in a crowded hall in Jurong. Haziq, the youngest member, was in charge of the robot's arm.
In the first round, the robot rolled forward smoothly, picked up one cup, then another. Then, with a harsh click, the arm dropped limply to the side. The judge's stopwatch kept running. "The spring snapped," whispered Mei Yi, the team leader. Haziq felt his face turn hot. He had been the one to tighten that spring the night before.
"I'm sorry," he mumbled. Nobody replied. Mei Yi was already searching her bag. She pulled out a thick red rubber band, looped it around the arm's joint and tested it. It sagged, but the arm lifted. "It won't be strong," she said. "We'll have to be gentle."
In the second round, Haziq guided the robot slowly, as if carrying a bowl of soup. It stacked three cups and then stopped. In the end, the team came third, behind two schools whose robots had cost much more.
On the bus home, Haziq stared out of the window. "We lost because of me," he said. Mei Yi shook her head. "We came third because of the rubber band. And because you moved the arm so carefully that it didn't snap again." Haziq laughed weakly and, for the first time that day, sat up straight.

What was the robot supposed to do?
options: Carry a bowl of soup across the hall
Stack plastic cups into a tower
Race around a track as fast as it could
Sort cups by colour into boxes

explain.why: Haziq moved the arm 'as if carrying a bowl of soup', but this was only a comparison.
The task was about picking up and stacking cups, not racing.
Sorting is not mentioned. It had to build a tower.

solution: The Robotics Club had spent three months building a robot that could pick up plastic cups and stack them into a tower.
This sentence states the robot's task.

A few years ago, smooth-coated otters surprised Singaporeans by appearing in the city. Today, families of otters can be seen at Marina Bay, along the Kallang River and even in some housing estates. Once, otters had almost vanished from Singapore because their homes by the water were polluted, and they could not find enough fish to eat. As the rivers became cleaner, the fish returned, and the otters followed.
An otter family can have as many as ten members, led by a mother and a father. The older brothers and sisters help to look after the pups. Otters hunt together, circling a school of fish so that none can escape. They have thick, waterproof fur that keeps them warm, and they groom it carefully after every meal.
Residents have mixed feelings about their new neighbours. Many enjoy watching the playful animals and taking photographs. Others worry. Otters have been known to enter ponds and eat the expensive fish of garden owners. Also, some visitors get too close to take pictures, which may frighten the otters, and a frightened otter may bite.
Experts therefore give simple advice: keep at least five metres away, do not feed them and never block their path to the water. With a little care, people and otters can share the city peacefully.

Why had otters almost vanished from Singapore?
options: Polluted water and a lack of fish to eat
The weather became too cold for them
Cars knocked down many of them on the roads
Hunters caught too many of them

explain.why: Weather is not mentioned.
The passage does not mention roads or cars.
Hunting is not mentioned. Pollution and lack of food are given.

solution: Once, otters had almost vanished from Singapore because their homes by the water were polluted, and they could not find enough fish to eat.
This sentence gives the reason.

On Saturday, Ah Ma decided it was time to teach Kai how to make ondeh-ondeh. "Your cousins know how already," she said, tying an apron around his waist. "It's your turn." Kai groaned under his breath. He would rather have played video games.
Ah Ma set a bowl of green dough on the counter. "Flatten a piece in your palm," she said. "Put the gula melaka inside. Then roll it closed, like this." Kai's first ball tore at the side, and the palm sugar dribbled onto the table. His second was too thick. His third looked like a lumpy potato. "It looks so ugly," he sighed.
Ah Ma did not scold. "My mother's looked ugly too," she said, "the first year." She pinched a bit of dough and showed him how to seal the edges slowly. Kai tried again. By the tenth ball, his fingers had learned to be gentle. The balls were round and plump.
They dropped them into boiling water. When the balls floated up, Ah Ma scooped them out and rolled them in fresh grated coconut. Kai bit into one. A burst of warm sugar filled his mouth, and he could not help smiling. "Ah Ma," he said, "can we make more tomorrow?" She chuckled. "Tomorrow," she said, "you can teach me how to play your games."

What goes inside the ondeh-ondeh balls?
options: Grated coconut
Sweet red bean paste
Gula melaka
Crushed peanuts and sugar

explain.why: Grated coconut is rolled on the outside after the balls are cooked.
The filling is gula melaka, not red bean paste.
Peanuts are not mentioned.

solution: "Put the gula melaka inside. Then roll it closed, like this."
Ah Ma says the gula melaka goes inside.

When Ms Lau announced that Sarah had won the Mathematics Excellence Award, the class erupted in applause. Wen Xin clapped too, but a beat late, and her smile felt like a mask fixed on with glue. All year, she had been the one who finished the problem sums first. Now a certificate with Sarah's name on it would be pinned to the wall for everyone to see.
At recess, Sarah hurried over, holding out half of her packet of cheese crackers. "Do you want to come to the library after this? I need help with the fractions revision." Wen Xin examined her fingernails. "I'm busy," she said. It was not true. She walked off, and the corridor seemed to stretch longer than usual.
That evening, Wen Xin stared at her homework and heard her mother humming in the kitchen. She remembered something that she wished she could forget. Last term, when she had been sick for a week, Sarah had come to her flat every afternoon with notes, copying each page by hand so that Wen Xin would not fall behind. Nobody had asked her to. She had even drawn a little smiling sun in the corner of each page.
Wen Xin slid open her bag and found that sun on the top page of her maths file. A hot, uncomfortable feeling crept into her chest. It was no longer envy, but shame. The next morning, she was waiting at the library door when Sarah arrived. "I'm free now," she said, a little stiffly. "Show me what you're stuck on." Sarah's face lit up like a lamp. They sat down together, and for the first time in weeks, the numbers on the page did not look so cold.

What did Sarah do when Wen Xin was sick?
options: She took Wen Xin's place in the class competition
She hand-copied notes and brought them over
She asked Ms Lau to excuse Wen Xin from homework
She taught the lessons to Wen Xin over the telephone

explain.why: No competition substitute is mentioned.
Nothing is said about Ms Lau excusing homework.
Telephone lessons are not mentioned. Sarah brought handwritten notes.

solution: Sarah had come to her flat every afternoon with notes, copying each page by hand so that Wen Xin would not fall behind.
The sentence describes Sarah's help.

On the rooftops and in the empty spaces between HDB blocks, vegetables are growing. Community gardens, once a rare sight, now thrive in many Singapore neighbourhoods. Residents plant chilli, kangkong and sweet potato, sharing tools and harvests. The gardens are tended by volunteers, many of them retirees who say the work keeps them active.
Supporters argue that the gardens do more than produce vegetables. They give neighbours a reason to talk to one another. Teachers bring pupils to see how vegetables grow, because a pupil who has tasted a chilli grown downstairs is more likely to remember where food comes from. The plants also cool their surroundings: a green wall can be several degrees cooler than a bare one.
Yet the gardens also face challenges. A garden needs steady attention, and when volunteers move away or grow tired, weeds soon spread and the plants wither. Some residents also complain that watering the plants attracts mosquitoes. In one estate, a patch had to be cleared after several complaints.
Still, the coordinators of the best-run gardens have found a few solutions. They draw up a watering schedule so that no one person is overburdened, and they ask residents to empty any standing water every week. Some gardens invite pupils to adopt a plot, ensuring that a new generation of gardeners is ready to take over.
The vegetables will never feed a whole estate, and few would claim otherwise. But a garden's real harvest, as one volunteer put it, may be the neighbours who finally learned each other's names.

Who looks after the community gardens?
options: Shoppers who buy the vegetables
Volunteers, many of them retirees
Paid workers from the town council
Teachers who bring their classes on visits

explain.why: The vegetables are harvested and shared by residents. Shoppers are not mentioned.
The passage says volunteers tend the gardens.
Teachers bring pupils to see the gardens. They are not said to run them.

solution: The gardens are tended by volunteers, many of them retirees who say the work keeps them active.
The sentence names those who tend the gardens.

By half past five every morning, the aroma of frying garlic had already drifted down to the carpark. Uncle Seng's chicken rice stall had been in the corner of the Block 12 hawker centre for thirty-one years, and I had grown up on its steaming plates. This morning, I was helping while my father, Uncle Seng's nephew, drove a delivery van.
Uncle Seng worked in silence, his old hands moving without hurry. He cut the chicken in clean, even slices, ladled the sauce, and flicked a sprig of coriander on each plate like a signature. "No two plates are the same," he said, "but each must be right." A queue had formed, and the customers did not seem to mind the wait.
At nine, when the rush slowed, a young man in a pressed shirt walked up. He was Uncle Seng's son, Daryl, who worked in an office downtown. "Pa, you're seventy-one," he said, in the careful voice of someone who had rehearsed. "The rent is going up. Why don't you rest?" Uncle Seng wiped his hands slowly. "And who would cook for them?" he asked, nodding at a regular, an old man who was already eating his second helping. "Can your office do that?"
Daryl said nothing for a while. Then he took the apron off the nail on the wall and put it on. "Show me the sauce," he said. Uncle Seng looked at him over the top of his spectacles, and something in his weathered face seemed to loosen. "The sauce," he said, "takes thirty years. But we can begin with the chilli."
I returned to washing the bowls, pretending not to hear, but my own eyes stung a little.

Fifty-one years
Seventy-one years
Thirty-one years

explain.why: Thirty years is how long Uncle Seng says the sauce takes to learn.
This number does not appear in the passage.
Seventy-one is Uncle Seng's age.

solution: Uncle Seng's chicken rice stall had been in the corner of the Block 12 hawker centre for thirty-one years, and I had grown up on its steaming plates.
The sentence gives the number of years.

Every afternoon at four, I practised the violin. For three weeks, I had been struggling with the same eight bars of a Bach minuet, and each time I reached the third bar, the bow squealed like a frightened cat. On the Thursday of the third week, a sharp knock rattled our door.
Mdm Rosli from next door stood in the corridor, her arms folded. "Your son's music," she said to my mother, "is not beautiful." Mum apologised three times and promised that I would practise only on weekends. When she closed the door, she looked at me with the weary expression she wore when bills arrived. I put the violin in its case and snapped the lid shut harder than I needed to.
For two weeks, the flat was silent in the afternoons. I told myself I was relieved. But on the second Thursday of the silence, when the clock struck four, I found myself standing by the case with my hand on the clasp, listening to the quiet.
There was another knock. This time, it was gentle. Mdm Rosli held a plate of curry puffs wrapped in foil. Her eyes did not meet mine. "I was unwell last month," she said, "and the squeaking made my head ache. But the quiet is worse." She cleared her throat. "The third bar. You still squeak there."
"I know," I said.
"Then play it again," she said, "until you don't."

What did Mdm Rosli bring on her second visit?
options: A written complaint to the town council
A bag of oranges
A plate of curry puffs
A new set of violin strings

explain.why: She complained by knocking on the door the first time. No letter is mentioned.
The gift was curry puffs.
Violin strings are not mentioned.

solution: Mdm Rosli held a plate of curry puffs wrapped in foil.
The sentence names the gift.

For years, walkers and cyclists have shared the park connectors that run through many of Singapore's neighbourhoods, and for years the two groups have grumbled about each other. Walkers complain that cyclists whizz past without warning. Cyclists reply that walkers drift across the path, earphones in, unaware.
Last year, the authorities tried an experiment on a two-kilometre stretch. A painted line divided the path into two lanes, one for cyclists and one for walkers. Signs asked cyclists to ring their bells before overtaking and set a speed limit of ten kilometres an hour. Volunteers in orange vests stood at busy corners to remind users of the rules.
The early results were encouraging. In the first three months, the number of reported near-misses fell by almost half. Most walkers said they felt safer. However, many cyclists felt the lane was too narrow for them to pass slower riders, and some riders ignored the speed limit once the volunteers had left. Meanwhile, a group of parents with prams pointed out that the walkers' lane was sometimes crowded, forcing them to step on to the cycling lane.
Planners say that the trial shows rules alone are not enough. They are now looking at widening the busiest stretches and adding rest areas where cyclists can stop and drink water without blocking others. "A path is a shared space," one planner remarked. "The goal is not to separate people, but to help them notice each other."

Which step was part of the trial?
options: Banning bicycles on weekends
Setting up cameras to fine speeding riders
Charging cyclists a fee to use the path
Painting a line to split the path

explain.why: No ban is mentioned.
Volunteers reminded users of the rules. Cameras and fines are not mentioned.
Fees are not mentioned.

solution: A painted line divided the path into two lanes, one for cyclists and one for walkers.
This sentence describes the main change made in the trial.

The baton slipped from Rizwan's fingers on the last bend and hit the track with a hollow clack that seemed to echo around the entire stadium. For one long second, nobody moved. Then the other teams streaked past, and Rizwan's legs, which had felt so springy a moment ago, felt as heavy as sandbags.
He bent down, snatched up the baton and ran, but it was far too late. Our team crossed the finish line in last place. In the stands, our classmates fell silent, and the school banner drooped.
Afterwards, Rizwan sat alone on the bench, his towel over his head. I knew that the rest of us had been practising the baton changes since January. I also knew that Rizwan had been the one who stayed back on rainy days to rehearse the handover again and again.
Coach Mdm Goh crouched in front of him. "Look at me," she said. Rizwan shook his head. "I dropped it," came his muffled voice. "I know," she answered. "And I dropped the baton at a national meet when I was fourteen. I did not get a medal that year either, but I learnt something. The baton is not as important as what you do after it falls." She paused. "You picked it up and finished the race. Many runners just walk off."
Slowly, Rizwan lowered the towel. His eyes were red, but he was looking at her. Behind him, the rest of us gathered quietly, and I placed my hand on his shoulder. Nobody said anything more. We did not need to.

Where did the baton slip from Rizwan's fingers?
options: After he crossed the finish line
During a handover to the second runner
On the last bend
On the first bend

explain.why: He picked it up and carried on running, so he had not yet finished.
The baton fell on the last bend, while Rizwan was running.
The passage says the last bend.

solution: The baton slipped from Rizwan's fingers on the last bend and hit the track with a hollow clack that seemed to echo around the entire stadium.
The first sentence states where it slipped.
